answer.label: Not Leonardo da Vinci — actually Thomas Paine
answer.sourceLine: The line is a reworded excerpt from Thomas Paine’s “The American Crisis,” No. I, published December 1776. Paine actually wrote “I love the man that can smile in trouble” — the internet softened it to “those who” and re-credited it to Leonardo da Vinci, who never wrote it.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: “I love the man that can smile in trouble”

source.excerpt: I love the man that can smile in trouble, that can gather strength from distress, and grow brave by reflection. ’Tis the business of little minds to shrink; but he whose heart is firm, and whose conscience approves his conduct, will pursue his principles unto death.
trail: The exact wording surfaces attributed to Leonardo da Vinci across quote sites — e.g. this Goodreads entry, which even pluralizes the rest of Paine’s sentence.

But the passage belongs to Thomas Paine: Wikiquote’s sourced text of The American Crisis gives “I love the man that can smile in trouble, that can gather strength from distress, and grow brave by reflection.”
The full pamphlet in The Writings of Thomas Paine, Vol. I (Project Gutenberg) confirms the line in Crisis No. I, opposite the famous opening “These are the times that try men’s souls.”
source.excerptNote: Paine’s original text. The viral “Leonardo” version rewrites “the man that” as “those who” and pluralizes the rest.

author.name: Thomas Paine
author.heading: About Thomas Paine
author.bio: Thomas Paine was an English-born writer whose pamphlets helped ignite the American Revolution. Common Sense (1776) argued for independence, and The American Crisis (begun December 1776) rallied a faltering Continental Army — Washington had its first number read aloud to his troops before the crossing of the Delaware. The “smile in trouble” line is Paine’s, not Leonardo’s.

misattribution.heading: How Leonardo got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” swap: a stirring line by a real author gets softened and re-credited to a more glamorous one.

items.why: Countless quote sites (BrainyQuote, Goodreads) pin this on Leonardo, but none cite any notebook, treatise, or letter of his — because the words are Paine’s, written more than 250 years after Leonardo’s death.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Thomas Paine’s, from The American Crisis, No. I (1776) — and his original reads “I love the man that can smile in trouble,” not “those who.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Paine wrote the first Crisis paper in the darkest weeks of 1776, as Washington’s army retreated across New Jersey. The “smile in trouble” sentence sits a few lines below its famous opening, “These are the times that try men’s souls.”
Stripped of that revolutionary context and softened into a gentle life-coach maxim, the line reads like timeless Renaissance wisdom — which is likely why it drifted onto Leonardo da Vinci’s name.
